title: Predation, more often than food supply, sets average numbers

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Predation, more often than food supply, sets average numbers

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Although food sets the upper limit to a species' increase, very often it is destruction by predators rather than food supply that determines the species' average numbers.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The amount of food for each species of course gives the extreme limit to which each can increase; but very frequently it is not the obtaining food, but the serving as prey to other animals, which determines the average numbers of a species.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter III, “Struggle for Existence”; section “Nature of the checks to increase”. Scope: animal populations in nature, e.g. game birds and mammals

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch03-04: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.54

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Population and interaction databases identify candidate systems, but the causal covariates needed to distinguish predation from food limitation are sparse. Existing data can resolve selected long-term studies only.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Across animal population time series, compare variance and density dependence attributable to prey resources versus predator abundance using lagged causal models or removals. More populations primarily limited by predation would support 'very frequently.'

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Top-down and bottom-up effects interact and share climate drivers.

Food and predator time series rarely accompany focal abundance.

fields.value:

discriminating power: 0.51
data adequacy: 0.34

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The contrast between predator and food effects is operationally clear and has been meta-analysed in the literature, but the public experimental tables are incomplete. Nutrient-addition data are the strongest open piece and address only the food side, mostly for plants. A frequency judgment of 'very often' across animal populations would require compiling a biased, study-level sample.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare effect sizes of predator removal and of food supplementation on equilibrium density across field experiments. Predation determining average numbers 'very frequently' would be supported if predator treatments changed density more often, or by more, than food treatments, while food still set an upper bound in enrichment studies; the reverse pattern would count against the frequency claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Predator-exclusion results are scattered across papers rather than one open experiment archive.

Nutrient-network data cover plants, whereas the clearest predation claim is about animals.

Food and predation interact, and short experiments miss the upper food limit.

discriminating power: 0.5
data existence: 0.46
